text:
A Bullion Trading Tradition
Las Arras Matrimoniales
Las Arras & Mexican Gold — the 13 Wedding Coins
Thirteen small coins, passed hand to hand at the altar, carry one of the oldest promises in the Hispanic Catholic wedding. Behind that keepsake sits a much larger Mexican love affair with gold — the Centenario and the Hidalgo pesos. Here is what the thirteen coins mean, and the real gold families gift for a lifetime.
Educational only — the ceremonial arras set is a symbolic keepsake; customs vary by family and parish.
MÉXICO
50
CENTENARIO
Thirteen small coins, passed hand to hand at the altar, carry one of the oldest promises in the Hispanic Catholic wedding:
I will provide, and I will share everything I have with you.
They are called
las arras matrimoniales
— the marital pledge — and behind that keepsake sits a much larger Mexican love affair with gold.
This is a plain-English guide to what the thirteen coins mean, who gives them, and what they are actually made of — and to the real, enduring gold that Mexican families have gifted for generations: the
Centenario
and its smaller siblings, the Hidalgo pesos.
Coins in a set

What las arras matrimoniales are
Las arras
— from the Spanish for “earnest money” or “pledge” — are thirteen coins exchanged during a Catholic wedding Mass. Traditionally the groom pours them into the bride’s cupped hands as a spoken promise that he will provide for her and their future family; her acceptance signals trust in that promise. Many couples today exchange the coins back and forth, expressing a shared, equal partnership.
In the order of the ceremony, las arras usually follow the exchange of rings and precede the finalizing of the vows. The priest blesses the coins before they change hands, and they are presented in an ornate box or chest called a
cofre
. The custom is old — commonly traced to the Roman
arrha
(earnest money that sealed a betrothal) and to the marriage rites of Visigothic Spain — and Spain carried it across the Atlantic to Mexico and Latin America, and to the Philippines.
Las arras — thirteen coins, blessed and passed hand to hand, presented in the
cofre
. In the mass-market set they are gold-tone keepsakes; some families use real gold instead.
The number thirteen is the heart of the symbol, and three readings are all in circulation:
Reading
Meaning
Jesus + the 12 apostles
The most common Catholic interpretation
12 months + 1 for the poor
An older folk reading — the thirteenth coin is a call to charity
13 shared values
A modern reading — the values the couple pledges to share
Why the set contains exactly thirteen coins.
Who gives the arras — the padrinos
In Mexican and Mexican-American weddings, sponsors called
padrinos
and
madrinas
underwrite meaningful parts of the celebration. The
padrino
and
madrina de arras
are the sponsors responsible for the coins: they buy the set, often choose it together, and present it at the altar. It is precisely this sponsor role — someone looking for a meaningful, lasting gift — where the choice of
what the coins are made of
becomes an interesting one.
The padrinos present the coins
The padrino and madrina de arras choose and buy the set, and carry the cofre to the altar; a young coin bearer — the arras equivalent of a ring bearer — sometimes brings it up the aisle.
The priest blesses the thirteen
Before the coins change hands, the priest blesses them — the moment that sets the arras apart from an ordinary gift.
The coins pass, hand to hand
The groom, or both partners, let the thirteen coins fall from one set of cupped hands into the other — a promise meant to be seen and heard by everyone present.
What the coins are made of — an honest look
Here is the plain truth many wedding sites gloss over: the standard, widely-sold thirteen-coin arras set is a
keepsake, not bullion
. The coins are typically gold-tone, gold- or silver-plated base metal, and the cofre is a plated or resin box, often set with rhinestones. Popular sets — many bearing the image of the Virgen de Guadalupe — sell for roughly
$20 to $80
. Their value is entirely symbolic, and that is exactly as intended: the ritual carries the meaning.
Some families instead choose
real silver or gold coins
, or heirloom coins handed down through the family. That is a matter of taste and means, not liturgical requirement. When a family wants the arras to be genuinely precious — or wants a separate, enduring gift to mark the wedding — they step out of the decorative-keepsake market and into real bullion. In Mexican culture, that path leads almost inevitably to one coin.

The Centenario — Mexico’s iconic gold coin
The
50 Peso gold coin
, universally called the
Centenario
, was first struck in
1921
to mark the
centenario
— the 100th anniversary — of Mexico’s independence, dated from the 1810 uprising led by Miguel Hidalgo. It is one of the most substantial gold coins ever produced for circulation and investment: a gross weight of
41.6666 grams
, of which
37.5 grams is pure gold
— an actual gold weight of
1.2057 troy ounces
at
.900 fineness
, about 37 mm across. That is more gold than a one-ounce Gold Eagle or Krugerrand, part of its appeal as a statement gift.
MÉXICO
50
CENTENARIO · ORO
The Centenario’s obverse shows the Ángel de la Independencia — Mexico City’s Winged Victory — framed by laurel, with the coat of arms on the reverse.
The obverse shows the
Ángel de la Independencia
— the Winged Victory known as “El Ángel” that crowns the monument on Mexico City’s Paseo de la Reforma — holding a laurel wreath and broken chains, standing before the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl. The reverse bears Mexico’s coat of arms: the golden eagle on a nopal cactus, devouring a serpent.
One quirk every buyer should know: most Centenarios you will meet are dated
1947
. That is a “frozen” restrike date. The original 1921 issue was only about 180,000 coins; from the late 1940s onward the Mexican Mint kept striking coins bearing the 1947 date to satisfy demand, producing millions more over the decades. So a “1947” Centenario may have been minted long after 1947 — which is why the coin is plentiful, liquid, and priced closely to its gold content.
The Hidalgo series — smaller gold pesos
The Centenario has a family of smaller siblings, most bearing the portrait of independence hero
Miguel Hidalgo
, all struck in the same
.900 fine
gold. They let a family give real Mexican gold at a range of price points — the 50 / 20 / 10 / 5 / 2.5 peso ladder that has long made gold pesos a
patrimonio
: a store of value you can start small, add to, and pass on.

The wider culture — gold for life’s milestones
Gifting gold at sacramental milestones runs deep in Mexican Catholic life. At a
quinceañera
— a girl’s 15th birthday and passage into young womanhood — godparents traditionally present blessed gifts: a rosary, a medal, or a gold necklace with a pendant of the
Virgen de Guadalupe
, often meant as an heirloom. At a
baptism
and first communion, the padrinos again give a religious medal or a small piece of gold.
And on
December 12, the Día de la Virgen de Guadalupe
— the feast of Mexico’s patron saint, a national holiday since 1859 — gold Guadalupe medals and coins are among the season’s most cherished gifts. Across all of these — wedding, quinceañera, baptism, Guadalupe — the through-line is the same: gold as a way to make a blessing tangible, and to hand faith and security from one generation to the next.
Give real Mexican gold
We don’t sell the ceremonial plated arras set — that belongs to the bridal shop, and it’s perfect for the ritual. But if you’re a padrino, a parent, or a couple who wants to mark the occasion with something
real and lasting
, the Centenario and the Hidalgo pesos are exactly what we carry, and we ship nationwide.

Common Questions
Questions families ask us
What are las arras matrimoniales?
They are thirteen wedding coins exchanged during a Mexican or Hispanic Catholic wedding Mass. The groom traditionally gives them to the bride as a promise to provide for and share everything with their household; many modern couples exchange them mutually as a sign of equal partnership. A priest usually blesses the coins first.
Why are there exactly 13 coins?
The most common Catholic reading is that they represent Jesus and the twelve apostles. An older folk interpretation sees the twelve months of the year plus a thirteenth coin set aside for the poor, a reminder of charity. Many couples today treat them as thirteen values they promise to share.
Who buys and gives the arras?
Traditionally the padrinos de arras — the wedding sponsors, a godfather (padrino) and godmother (madrina) — purchase the coin set and present it at the altar. A young coin bearer, like a ring bearer, sometimes carries the cofre (box) up the aisle.
Are the arras coins real gold?
Usually not. The standard, mass-market thirteen-coin arras set is a symbolic keepsake made of gold-tone, gold-plated, or silver-plated base metal, sold for roughly $20–$80 with a decorative box. That is by design — the meaning is in the ritual. Some families instead choose real silver or gold coins, or heirloom coins, if they want the arras to be genuinely precious.
What is the Centenario, and how much gold is in it?
The Centenario is Mexico’s iconic 50 Peso gold coin, first struck in 1921 for the 100th anniversary of independence. It contains 37.5 grams of pure gold — 1.2057 troy ounces — in a 41.6666-gram coin of .900 fine gold, about 37 mm across. That is more gold than a one-ounce Gold Eagle or Krugerrand.
Why are so many Centenarios dated 1947?
1947 is a “frozen” restrike date. The original 1921 mintage was only about 180,000 coins, but from the late 1940s onward the Mexican Mint kept producing coins bearing the 1947 date to meet investor demand — millions of them over the following decades. So a “1947” Centenario may actually have been minted long after 1947. This is why the coin is common, liquid, and priced close to its gold content.
What smaller Mexican gold coins are available as gifts?
The Hidalgo series offers real gold at lower price points, all at .900 fineness: the 20 Pesos (0.4823 oz), 10 Pesos (0.2411 oz), 5 Pesos (0.1206 oz), and 2.5 Pesos (0.0603 oz). The smaller pieces make giftable, genuine-gold keepsakes for a baptism or quinceañera.
When do Mexican families traditionally gift gold?
At weddings and quinceañeras (a girl’s 15th birthday), at baptisms and first communions, and around December 12, the Día de la Virgen de Guadalupe, Mexico’s patron saint. Gold Guadalupe medals, jewelry, and coins are given as blessed, heirloom gifts meant to pass faith and security to the next generation.
Marking a wedding, quinceañera, or baptism?
Whether you are a padrino starting a family patrimonio or giving one enduring blessing, we can help you choose the Mexican gold coin that fits the occasion — the Centenario, a 20 Peso, or a small Hidalgo piece — and ship it nationwide.
